summary: A change notice for IMP system version 2514, scheduled for installation in January 1972. It fixes problems with the delay applied after a host comes up, backing it off to 30 seconds and removing an ambiguity that could make it far longer.

plainLanguage.summary: The network box's waiting time was too long and unclear, so it is going back to a shorter, clear wait.

questions: what is the imp delay when a host comes online
why did version 2514 change the host delay
what must a host do when coming alive on the network
subtitle: A fix to the IMP startup timing that was confusing hosts

tldr.problem: The IMP system version 2513 had a confusing delay rule when hosts came online, with the delay sometimes lasting much longer than expected.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 271 announces IMP version 2514, which reduces the delay from over 40 seconds back to 30 seconds and removes the ambiguity in how the delay is applied.
tldr.outcome: The clearer timing helps hosts come online reliably without hardware difficulties, though hosts must still be ready to receive packets immediately.

today: RFC 271 is a historical record of early ARPANET infrastructure operations and has not been obsoleted. It documents the operational decisions that shaped how hosts joined the network.

sections.title: The IMP Update
sections.content: RFC 271 announces a new version of the IMP system (version 2514) scheduled for installation on January 13, 1972. The IMP is the network box that connects hosts to the ARPANET. This version addresses problems with version 2513 related to the delay period when a host comes online.
sections.plainLanguage: A new version of the network box is being installed to fix timing problems.

sections.title: The Problem with Version 2513
sections.content: Version 2513 had two problems with the delay between when a host indicates it is coming online and when the IMP accepts the second packet from that host. First, the delay was too long at over 40 seconds, causing hardware difficulties at some sites. Second, there was an ambiguity in how the delay was measured that could allow it to stretch as long as 75 seconds, far longer than intended.
sections.plainLanguage: The waiting time was too long and confusing—sometimes it could wait way longer than it should.

sections.title: The Fix and Host Requirement
sections.content: Version 2514 reduces the delay back to 30 seconds and eliminates the ambiguity entirely. However, hosts must understand a critical requirement: immediately after signaling that they are alive, they must be ready to accept all messages from the network, even during the 30-second waiting period. If a host does not accept messages immediately, the IMP may drop its ready line briefly as part of its normal interface checking procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The delay is now a clear 30 seconds, but hosts have to be ready to receive messages right away, not wait for the delay to finish.

references.text: BBN Report 1822, Specifications for the Interconnection of a Host and an IMP
